name: Binary Analysis & Reverse Engineering
description: Disassembly, decompilation, binary similarity, and reverse engineering of compiled code.

ccs.narrative:
Research on binary analysis at CCS began taking shape around 2018, with early work concentrating on binary analysis, decompilation, reverse engineering, and binary hardening. Debin: Predicting Debug Information in Stripped Binaries (CCS 2018) set an influential baseline by showing how to Uses machine learning to predict debug information like names and types in stripped binaries. Parallel contributions—Block Oriented Programming: Automating Data-Only Attacks (2018) and Towards Paving the Way for Large-Scale Windows Malware Analysis: Generic Binary Unpacking with Orders-of-Magnitude Performance Boost (2018) —reinforced the foundational challenges in this space.

A productive wave of CCS work from 2020–2022 deepened the area. Other strong contributions included SymLM: Predicting Function Names in Stripped Binaries via Context-Sensitive Execution-Aware Code Embeddings (2022), FirmXRay: Detecting Bluetooth Link Layer Vulnerabilities From Bare-Metal Firmware (2020), broadening the space of techniques and targets.

The most recent CCS contributions (from 2023 onward) reflect a maturing field that pushes into harder targets and broader threat models. ReSym: Harnessing LLMs to Recover Variable and Data Structure Symbols from Stripped Binaries (CCS 2024) exemplified this trend by tackling Uses LLMs to recover variable names and data-structure symbols from stripped binaries during decompilation. Similarly, Simplifying Mixed Boolean-Arithmetic Obfuscation by Program Synthesis and Term Rewriting (2023) and PackGenome: Automatically Generating Robust YARA Rules for Accurate Malware Packer Detection (2023) show how the community continues to scale and adapt its methods.

ndss.narrative:
Binary analysis at NDSS has progressed from foundational disassembly and taint inference toward deep-learning-assisted understanding of stripped code. Superset Disassembly (NDSS 2018) removed heuristics from x86 rewriting by exhaustively treating every byte offset as a potential instruction, establishing a clean baseline. Contemporaneously, cross-architecture taint-rule inference (One Engine To Serve 'em All, NDSS 2019) automated the labor-intensive annotation required for multi-ISA analysis.

The 2020–2022 period introduced learned representations and firmware-specific tooling. DeepBinDiff (NDSS 2020) applied program-wide embeddings to binary diffing with unprecedented granularity; NetPlier (NDSS 2021) used probabilistic inference over message traces to reverse-engineer network protocols; FirmWire (NDSS 2022) delivered a transparent dynamic-analysis and fuzzing platform for cellular baseband firmware, making a previously opaque attack surface accessible.

The most recent wave (2023–2025) has been defined by the entry of large language models. DeGPT (NDSS 2024) showed LLMs can refine decompiler output into more readable pseudocode; VulHawk (NDSS 2023) combined entropy-based search with cross-architecture vulnerability detection; and Beyond Classification: Inferring Function Names in Stripped Binaries via Domain Adapted LLMs (NDSS 2025) demonstrated that LLM fine-tuning can recover semantic labels lost during compilation. The field has shifted from heuristic-free static analysis to semantics-aware ML-augmented reverse engineering.

sp.narrative:
Binary analysis at IEEE S&P addresses the challenge of understanding and securing software without source code. The foundational 2019 paper, Asm2Vec: Boosting Static Representation Robustness for Binary Clone Search against Code Obfuscation and Compiler Optimization (S&P 2019), demonstrated that neural assembly embeddings could find code clones despite compiler transformation and deliberate obfuscation—a key step in making semantic binary analysis practical.

The 2020 cohort diversified targets and methods. RetroWrite: Statically Instrumenting COTS Binaries for Fuzzing and Sanitization (S&P 2020) solved binary rewriting for x86-64 position independent executables, enabling coverage-guided fuzzing on stripped binaries. Binsec/Rel: Efficient Relational Symbolic Execution for Constant-Time at Binary-Level (S&P 2020) verified constant-time properties of cryptographic implementations at the binary level, catching compiler-introduced timing side channels invisible at the source level.

From 2021, binary analysis expanded to decompilation and structured recovery. SoK: All You Ever Wanted to Know About x86/x64 Binary Disassembly But Were Afraid to Ask (S&P 2021) systematized disassembly error sources and tool trade-offs. OSPREY: Recovery of Variable and Data Structure via Probabilistic Analysis for Stripped Binary (S&P 2021) applied probabilistic inference to recover high-level variable types from stripped executables. StochFuzz: Sound and Cost-effective Fuzzing of Stripped Binaries by Incremental and Stochastic Rewriting (S&P 2021) addressed coverage instrumentation for binaries that cannot be statically rewritten.

By 2024, LLM-assisted decompilation appeared: 'Len or index or count, anything but v1': Predicting Variable Names in Decompilation Output with Transfer Learning (S&P 2024) used transfer learning to recover human-readable variable names from decompiler output, marking the field's embrace of neural methods for the last-mile reverse engineering challenge.

uss.narrative:
The earliest listed work in this area focused on wrestling control over real-world compiled systems where source code is unavailable or unwieldy. "Inception: System-Wide Security Testing of Real-World Embedded Systems Software" (USENIX 2018) tackled the messy reality of testing firmware-grade binaries, while "Precise and Accurate Patch Presence Test for Binaries" (USENIX 2018) showed you can tell whether a security patch made it into a shipped binary without source. Alongside these, "DATA - Differential Address Trace Analysis" (USENIX 2018) pushed binary analysis toward a precise security goal, hunting address-based side channels directly in compiled crypto code. The common thread: classic program-analysis problems re-framed for the stripped, optimized binaries that defenders and attackers actually face.

The next shift was twofold. First, researchers sharpened the core binary-analysis primitives and turned them against adversarial code: "DEEPVSA" (USENIX 2019) brought deep learning to value-set analysis for postmortem forensics, and a defensive sub-thread emerged with "Fuzzification: Anti-Fuzzing Techniques" and "AntiFuzz: Impeding Fuzzing Audits of Binary Executables" (both USENIX 2019), which deliberately make binaries harder to reverse and fuzz. Second, the field broadened its targets. "Everything Old is New Again: Binary Security of WebAssembly" (USENIX 2020) extended reverse-engineering concerns to a new compilation target, and a 2021 wave matured binary-only tooling: "Breaking Through Binaries" delivered compiler-quality instrumentation for binary fuzzing, "SelectiveTaint" made static-rewriting taint tracking efficient, and "DeepReflect" reconstructed malicious functionality from binaries. Obfuscation became a first-class battleground, with "MBA-Blast" (USENIX 2021) simplifying Mixed Boolean-Arithmetic obfuscation and "Loki" (USENIX 2022) hardening obfuscation against the automated attacks that work like MBA-Blast had enabled.

By 2022 the area pivoted hard toward learning-based binary understanding and, notably, toward studying the human reverse engineer. "How Machine Learning Is Solving the Binary Function Similarity Problem" (USENIX 2022) became a reference point for binary similarity, complemented by neural disassembly in "DeepDi" (USENIX 2022) and even neural-network decompilation in "DnD: A Cross-Architecture Deep Neural Network Decompiler" (USENIX 2022). At the same time, "RE-Mind" and "Decomperson" (both USENIX 2022) opened a human-factors line, asking how analysts actually decompile and reason, rather than only building tools.

Today the area sits at two frontiers. Embedded and firmware rehosting matured into practical pipelines, with "Greenhouse" and "FirmSolo" (both USENIX 2023) enabling dynamic analysis of IoT firmware and kernel modules, and "BASECOMP" (USENIX 2023) carrying these techniques into cellular baseband. Meanwhile, the quality of the abstractions we recover became the central question: "Code is not Natural Language" (USENIX 2024) pushed semantics-oriented graph representations for binary similarity, while "Ahoy SAILR!" and "A Taxonomy of C Decompiler Fidelity Issues" (both USENIX 2024) turned a critical eye on decompiler output itself, arguing for compiler-aware structuring and systematically cataloguing where decompiled C still falls short.

top4.narrative:
The earliest papers in this list, clustered in 2018, show binary analysis grappling with the foundational problem that compiled code throws away almost everything useful: symbols, types, structure, and even reliable instruction boundaries. Work like "Debin: Predicting Debug Information in Stripped Binaries" (CCS 2018) and "Using Logic Programming to Recover C++ Classes and Methods from Compiled Executables" (CCS 2018) tried to recover lost high-level information, while "Superset Disassembly: Statically Rewriting x86 Binaries Without Heuristics" (NDSS 2018) attacked the equally stubborn problem of just disassembling and rewriting x86 reliably. A parallel security-application thread appears in the same year — turning analysis into offense and defense, as in "Block Oriented Programming: Automating Data-Only Attacks" (CCS 2018) and the malware-focused unpacking and de-virtualization work like "VMHunt" (CCS 2018) and the Android unpacker study (NDSS 2018).

The clear breakthrough shift is the arrival of machine learning for binary representation. "Asm2Vec" (S&P 2019) was a watershed, showing that learned embeddings of assembly could survive obfuscation and compiler-optimization noise for clone search, and it triggered a wave: "DeepBinDiff" (NDSS 2020) for program-wide diffing and "PalmTree: Learning an Assembly Language Model for Instruction Embedding" (CCS 2021), which brought BERT-style pretraining to instructions. By 2022 the field paused to take stock with "How Machine Learning Is Solving the Binary Function Similarity Problem" (USENIX 2022), a sobering measurement study of what actually works.

Alongside the learning revolution, the systems-and-tooling side matured. "RetroWrite: Statically Instrumenting COTS Binaries for Fuzzing and Sanitization" (S&P 2020) and "Breaking Through Binaries" (USENIX 2021) pushed compiler-quality instrumentation into binary-only fuzzing, while "SymQEMU" (NDSS 2021) made symbolic execution practical on raw binaries. The community also consolidated hard-won knowledge in "SoK: All You Ever Wanted to Know About x86/x64 Binary Disassembly But Were Afraid to Ask" (S&P 2021) and even studied the humans doing the work in "RE-Mind: a First Look Inside the Mind of a Reverse Engineer" (USENIX 2022). A strong embedded/firmware vertical grew here too, from "FirmXRay" (CCS 2020) through "BaseSpec" (NDSS 2021) and "FirmWire" (NDSS 2022) for cellular basebands.

Where it stands now is a convergence of probabilistic recovery and large language models. Probabilistic structure recovery in "OSPREY" (S&P 2021) set the stage for LLM-driven approaches that now dominate the recovery problem: "DeGPT: Optimizing Decompiler Output with LLM" (NDSS 2024) and "ReSym: Harnessing LLMs to Recover Variable and Data Structure Symbols from Stripped Binaries" (CCS 2024) use LLMs to clean up decompiler output and recover symbols, while similarity research keeps refining its representations, as in "Code is not Natural Language" (USENIX 2024), which argues for semantics-oriented graphs over treating assembly as text. The throughline is consistent: recover what the compiler erased — boundaries, symbols, types, structure, and semantics — increasingly with learned and now LLM-based models, while building the rewriting and instrumentation plumbing that lets those analyses run on real-world stripped binaries.
